meta.title: Arabic B1
meta.subtitle: 800 words · Modern Standard Arabic · both directions
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Arabic → English (see the Arabic, recall the meaning) and English → Arabic (see an English meaning, recall the Arabic). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 800 words of Modern Standard Arabic — the written and formal language shared across the Arab world, not any one country's spoken dialect — for level B1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand the main points of clear standard input on familiar matters regularly encountered in work, school, leisure, etc.'. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no Arabic examination publishes an open graded word list, so this deck is not an exam board's vocabulary and does not claim to be. Every word was chosen for the level's topics — feelings and character; people and relationships; describing people; work and jobs; money and shopping; school and learning; the town, travel and holidays; health and the body; nature, animals and the weather; the media and technology; the world and society; culture and the arts; free time, sport and the media; the home; food, cooking and eating out; time and how often; little words; describing things; everyday verbs — and the cards are dealt by how often each word occurs in a frequency list built from Arabic film and television subtitles, the greetings first, so the words you meet most often come early. It builds on the levels below it: no word an earlier Arabic deck teaches is taught again here, so start with Arabic A1 and Arabic A2 if you have not. The words the earlier decks' lists held but left out as less common compete for a place here, so none of them is lost between levels. Every headword is printed WITH its short vowels, as books for learners print them, because Arabic is normally written without them and nothing in the bare spelling says how كتب is read. The example sentences are printed as they were written, which is mostly without vowels — the way Arabic is met in the world. Under every word on the back is its romanisation, in Wiktionary's scheme (ā ī ū for the long vowels, ʔ for hamza, ʕ for ʿayn, a dot under the emphatic letters), as a check on what the letters say rather than a substitute for them; the Arabic Alphabet deck teaches the letters first. 324 of the nouns show their plural, which in Arabic is mostly 'broken' (كِتَاب, كُتُب) and has to be learnt with the noun, and their gender; the 124 adjectives show their feminine, their plural and their comparative; the 211 verbs are named, as every Arabic dictionary names them, by the past tense 'he did' (كَتَبَ, 'to write'), with the present, the verbal noun and the verb's form (I–X) beside it, and a past and present table of eight persons behind the All forms fold. Real example sentences come with 723 of the 800 words, three apiece for 573, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. A sentence is matched by the word's own forms, with the little words Arabic writes joined to the front of a word (و 'and', بِ 'with', لِ 'for', the article الـ) allowed for; where two words of the deck share a spelling, a sentence is used only if its vowels say which one it is. Vowelled forms, romanisation, plurals and conjugations: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). The English meanings were written for this deck. Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR. The order: Hermit Dave's FrequencyWords, from OpenSubtitles (CC BY-SA 4.0).
